questions.q: A differential backup captures pages changed since which point?
options: Since the last full backup — not since the last differential backup
Since the last differential backup only
Since the database was created
Since the last log backup
questions.explain: Differentials always measure change relative to the last full backup. Each night's differential grows through the week until the next full resets it.

questions.q: What does a transaction log backup capture that a full or differential backup does not?
options: An ordered record of every transaction since the last log backup, which enables restoring to an exact point in time
A complete copy of every page in the database
Only the database schema, not the data
A copy of the server's configuration settings
questions.explain: Full and differential backups are snapshots of data pages. Log backups are a record of transactions in order, which is what makes point-in-time recovery possible.

questions.q: To restore a database using full, differential, and log backups, what is the correct restore order?
options: The last full backup, then the most recent differential taken after it, then every log backup since, in order
Only the most recent log backup — it contains everything
All differentials ever taken, from oldest to newest, then the full backup
Any order — SQL Server reconciles the order automatically
questions.explain: Restoring is a chain: full backup as the base, the latest differential on top of it, then every log backup since, applied in order.

questions.q: What happens if one log backup in the middle of a restore chain is missing or corrupted?
options: The restore chain breaks — you cannot apply the log backup after the missing one without it
SQL Server skips the missing log backup and continues automatically
Nothing — log backups are independent of each other
Only the differential backup becomes invalid, not the logs
questions.explain: Log backups form an unbroken chain. A missing link means every log backup after that point cannot be applied, which is the most common real-world backup failure.

questions.q: Why do log backups typically run far more often than full or differential backups in production?
options: Because they drive the recovery point objective — how much data loss is acceptable — which usually demands minutes, not a full day, between backups
Because log backups are much larger than full backups
Because SQL Server requires log backups to run every 5 minutes by default
Because differential backups replace the need for full backups entirely
questions.explain: Full and differential backups run on a coarse schedule (nightly, weekly), while log backups run continuously — often every 15 minutes to an hour — to keep the acceptable data-loss window small.
